note: Teacher's opinion about how often communication is neglected in design discussions; not a checkable fact.

Right that an HTTP endpoint is not automatically REST. But REST is not a 'specification': Fielding defines it as an architectural style, a set of constraints (client-server, stateless, cache, uniform interface, layered system, optional code-on-demand). No document defines a REST wire format. HTTP is the protocol most often used to build REST systems.
precise_version: REST is an architectural style, a set of constraints, defined in Roy Fielding's dissertation. HTTP is the protocol most often used to implement it, and an HTTP endpoint is not REST unless it follows those constraints.

note: Course/admin reference (the teacher's YouTube video). Not a technical claim.

Fine for teaching. Nuance: many engineers treat RPC (procedure-oriented, e.g. gRPC/Thrift) and REST (resource-oriented) as contrasting styles over HTTP. Calling every HTTP web server 'RPC' is a loose generic usage, not the usual industry framing.
Standard request-response description. The board's 'kept open with timeout' matches HTTP/1.1, where connections are persistent by default and idle connections are closed after a timeout.
Analogy; fine.
Correct definition of short polling.
Plausible illustration. How the AWS console actually refreshes instance state is not publicly documented.
Correct.
Plausible illustration. The transport Cricbuzz/ESPNcricinfo actually use is not publicly documented and may have changed.
Correct.

Arithmetic is correct: 6 req/min x 1M users = 6M req/min, about 100k req/s. Minor wording point: the transcript says '6 million concurrent requests per minute'. These are requests per minute, not concurrent requests.

Two issues. (1) TCP teardown is not 'two-way'. Each direction is closed independently with its own FIN, and each FIN is ACKed: FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK (four segments, sometimes three when FIN+ACK are combined), followed by TIME-WAIT. (2) Under HTTP/1.1, connections are persistent by default (keep-alive). Successive polls from a browser usually reuse an open TCP (and TLS) connection, so a new handshake per poll is the HTTP/1.0 model, not the norm. The real per-poll overhead is a full HTTP request/response with headers, plus server work for each poll, multiplied by the number of clients.
precise_version: Each short poll is a full HTTP request and response with headers. With HTTP/1.0-style short-lived connections, each poll also pays a TCP three-way handshake and a four-segment FIN/ACK teardown (plus a TLS handshake for HTTPS). HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 normally reuse a kept-alive connection, so the main cost is the request volume and header overhead, not new handshakes.

note: Correct: most polls return unchanged state, so the request volume is wasted.
Correct, and it matches RFC 6202's description: the server holds the request until an event, a status change, or a timeout, and the client then re-issues it immediately.

Partly true: you must write the application-specific 'has anything changed?' logic. But off-the-shelf long polling exists. Socket.IO falls back to HTTP long-polling automatically, and managed services expose it as a parameter (Amazon SQS ReceiveMessage WaitTimeSeconds, up to 20 s).
precise_version: Application-specific change detection is yours to write, but many libraries and services provide long polling as a ready-made transport or API option (e.g. Socket.IO's polling fallback, SQS WaitTimeSeconds).

note: The trade-off is right: far fewer requests, but the server holds an open request per client. Nuance: a well-built long-poll server does not busy-loop per request. It parks the request and wakes it from an event (pub/sub, condition variable, async future), and returns on timeout. RFC 6202 puts the main cost in holding a TCP connection and an HTTP request open per client. A per-request polling loop is an implementation choice and an anti-pattern at scale.

Same nuance as L-0248. The 'infinite loop in the backend' is one naive way to do it. Production systems usually notify waiting requests when the event (next ball) is published, instead of looping per request.
Correct comparison.
Reasonable claim. WebSockets are the dominant browser transport for chat and real-time apps.

Short polling is stateless at the protocol level. Long polling still makes the server hold a pending request (and its TCP connection) per client, so it is not purely stateless. The teacher hedges with 'kind of'.
Valid analogy: both reuse an established connection to avoid repeated handshakes.
Correct: a full-duplex channel over one TCP connection.

Partly right: RFC 6455 says WebSocket is 'an independent TCP-based protocol' and is not HTTP messages. But the opening handshake IS an HTTP/1.1 request (GET with Upgrade: websocket, answered by 101 Switching Protocols). By default it uses HTTP's ports 80/443 so it passes through HTTP infrastructure. RFC 8441 also runs WebSockets over a single HTTP/2 stream. 'Parallel to HTTP, not on top of it' can mislead readers into thinking HTTP proxies and load balancers are irrelevant. They must handle the Upgrade. WSS = WebSocket over TLS is correct.
precise_version: WebSocket is its own framing protocol over TCP, but it starts life as an HTTP/1.1 request that is 'upgraded' (101 Switching Protocols) on ports 80/443. After the handshake, frames are WebSocket, not HTTP. RFC 8441 also defines WebSockets over an HTTP/2 stream. WSS is WebSocket over TLS.

note: Correct: full-duplex, so the server can push at any time.
Correct canonical chat example.

Directionally right, but 'very expensive' needs context. An idle WebSocket costs mainly memory, a file descriptor, and per-connection state. Single servers have held over 2 million TCP connections (WhatsApp, 2012). The real costs are statefulness (routing, fan-out across nodes, reconnect storms, deploys that drop connections) and keepalives through proxies.
Course/admin reference.

Correct in spirit: there is no handshake per message, and frames are small (a 2-byte minimum header, up to 14 bytes with extended length and the client mask). Latency is still bounded by network RTT, so 'lightning speed' means no per-message connection setup or HTTP headers, not faster networking.
Plausible. Groww's and Robinhood's actual transports are not publicly documented in a primary source I could open.
Uses listed are standard WebSocket use cases. That Zoom chat specifically runs over WebSockets is not verifiable from a primary source.

MQTT is not a WebSocket variant. It is a lightweight publish/subscribe messaging protocol (broker-based) that runs over TCP/IP or another ordered, lossless, bi-directional transport, and MQTT 5.0 defines WebSocket as one such transport. It is mainly used for IoT and mobile messaging. Fast multiplayer games more often use custom UDP-based protocols.
precise_version: MQTT is a lightweight publish/subscribe messaging protocol over TCP (it can also be carried over WebSockets), popular for IoT. It is a different protocol from WebSocket, not a variant.

note: The first half is right: MQTT, WebSocket and HTTP are application-level specs running over a transport. But 'a persistent connection has to be TCP' is wrong. QUIC (RFC 9000) is a connection-oriented, stateful protocol carried in UDP datagrams, and HTTP/3 runs over it (RFC 9114). Games and VoIP keep long-lived sessions over UDP too. WebSocket and MQTT as specified do require an ordered, reliable byte stream (TCP or similar).
precise_version: Application protocols like HTTP, WebSocket and MQTT run on a transport. WebSocket and MQTT need a reliable, ordered stream, which is usually TCP. But long-lived connections are not TCP-only: QUIC builds persistent, encrypted connections on top of UDP, and HTTP/3 uses it.

note: Correct: unidirectional server-to-client over one long-lived HTTP response (text/event-stream). Nuances: (1) the client can still send data to the server with ordinary HTTP requests, just not over that stream. (2) The browser's EventSource reconnects automatically and sends Last-Event-ID so the server can resume.
Correct: the WHATWG spec calls them 'server-sent events'.
SSE suits log streaming and terminal-output streaming. Which transport specific vendors (Vercel, Netlify, the unclear 'Slice') use or used is not verifiable from a primary source.
Claim about vendors' internal history; not verifiable from primary sources.

SSE is widely consumed server-to-server today. For example, the Anthropic Messages API (and other LLM APIs) streams responses as server-sent events, which backend services consume directly. WebSockets are also used between services. 'Typically not done' is an outdated generalisation.
precise_version: SSE and WebSockets are most associated with browsers and devices, but they are also used between servers. A common modern case is streaming LLM API responses over SSE.

note: Correct overall. Nuances: SSE is text-only (UTF-8) with no binary frames. Over HTTP/1.1, browsers limit it to about 6 connections per domain across all tabs (not an issue over HTTP/2). WebSocket frame overhead itself is small, so the 'lightweight' advantage is mostly simplicity (plain HTTP, automatic reconnection), not bytes on the wire.

Rough figure. MDN's 'Using server-sent events' page has a short PHP server example (about 25-30 lines, including the client). The exact '21 lines' could not be confirmed and depends on the version of the page.

Good advice. Nuance for the Socket.IO suggestion: Socket.IO is not a WebSocket implementation. It adds its own packet metadata, falls back to HTTP long-polling, and a plain WebSocket client cannot talk to a Socket.IO server. To learn raw WebSockets, use the browser WebSocket API with a plain server library (e.g. ws).
Correct design description. DB drivers keep persistent TCP connections using the database's own wire protocol.
Reasonable design choice; see L-0279 for the common SSE + POST alternative.
Plausible examples. Twitter's and Instagram's actual transports are not verified from primary sources.

Partly right that the limits are physical/OS limits, but 'connected on ports' points at the wrong limit. A TCP connection is identified by the 4-tuple (src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port). A server listening on one port (e.g. 443) can hold millions of connections from different clients: WhatsApp reported over 2 million per server. The ephemeral-port limit (~28k-64k) bites the side that initiates connections to one destination (clients, proxies, LBs to a backend). The real server limits are file descriptors, memory per connection, CPU for keepalives/TLS, and conntrack/LB limits.
precise_version: No WebSocket-specific limit exists. On the server, the limits are file descriptors, memory and CPU, not ports: one listening port can hold millions of connections because each is identified by its 4-tuple. Port exhaustion is a problem for the connecting side (e.g. a proxy opening many connections to one backend).

note: The teacher is right that long polling can scale, much like long-lived connections. Nuances: each waiting client holds a TCP connection AND an HTTP request (RFC 6202). After every event all clients re-request at once, and proxies may cut long waits with 408/504. RFC 6202 suggests ~30 s timeouts. Scaling therefore needs an async/event-driven server, not one thread per waiting request.
Sound guidance. The 'not very long' wait matches RFC 6202's advice to keep long-poll timeouts around 30 s.

The student's proposal (likes sent as normal HTTP POSTs, counts pushed via SSE) is a valid, common pattern. The client doesn't need to send anything over the push channel. 'Plain SSE doesn't fit because users also send' doesn't rule it out; the teacher's 'you can do that' is the accurate part.
Correct: if the server dies, the held request fails and the client must retry. Retry safety (idempotency) depends on the use case.

Arithmetic is right (10,000 x 4 B = 40 KB). Nuances: real ticks also need an identifier, timestamp and framing, and prices are often not 4-byte ints. 40 KB/s per client x 1M clients is ~40 GB/s of egress, so server-side filtering or delta updates can matter at scale even if one client handles it easily.
Opinion/rule of thumb.

Correct: SSE is plain HTTP and works behind L7 load balancers. Watch idle timeouts and proxy buffering. The WHATWG spec recommends sending a comment line roughly every 15 s to keep proxies from dropping the connection.

Correct core point: your servers cannot push to a sleeping or killed mobile app directly. Delivery goes through the OS push service (APNs; FCM via Android's transport layer), which is outside your control and best-effort. Note that GCM was deprecated in 2018 and removed in 2019; it is now FCM.
Correct: apps schedule local notifications with time, calendar or location triggers, and the system delivers them without any server push.

'Push can be lost' is right: APNs is best-effort, stores only one pending notification per app, and may throttle. But the reasoning is backwards. The device DOES keep a persistent connection to the push service: Apple says devices 'need a persistent connection to Apple's servers' (TCP 5223, falling back to 443). The efficiency comes from the OS keeping ONE shared connection for all apps instead of each app keeping its own. Providers also keep long-lived HTTP/2 connections to APNs, and Apple says to reuse them 'for many hours to days'.
precise_version: Push notifications can be lost (APNs is best-effort and keeps only one pending notification per app). They are efficient because the operating system keeps a single persistent connection to the platform push service (APNs, or Google's Android transport for FCM) and multiplexes every app's notifications over it. Each app doesn't need its own connection.

note: Personal war story (2015, SNS delivery rates, OneSignal) - not judged.

The suggestion is now obsolete. Google deprecated GCM in April 2018 and its server and client APIs were removed starting April 11, 2019. Readers should integrate Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) instead (on Apple devices, FCM delivers through APNs).
precise_version: To learn native push, integrate once with Firebase Cloud Messaging (GCM's successor) and/or APNs directly, using their documentation.

note: Under HTTP/1.1 the connection is persistent by default and stays open after the response for reuse. It closes only on 'Connection: close' or an idle timeout. 'You explicitly break it after the response' describes HTTP/1.0's default short-lived model. The teacher's correction to the student (TCP under HTTP can be persistent) is right.
precise_version: HTTP/1.1 connections are persistent (keep-alive) by default and are reused for later requests. They are closed only when a side sends 'Connection: close' or the idle timeout expires. HTTP/1.0 closed after each response by default.

note: Right that app-to-DB traffic uses each database's own protocol over persistent TCP, not WebSockets. But 'dialect' is the wrong word. In ORMs and Go/Java libraries, a SQL dialect is the database's flavour of SQL syntax (e.g. Hibernate's Dialect, 'a dialect of SQL implemented by a particular RDBMS'). The byte-level format on the wire is the client/server wire protocol (MySQL Client/Server Protocol; PostgreSQL frontend/backend protocol on 5432).
precise_version: Each database has its own client/server wire protocol over TCP (e.g. MySQL protocol, PostgreSQL frontend/backend protocol, MongoDB wire protocol). Separately, ORMs pick a SQL 'dialect' so they generate SQL syntax that database understands.

note: The idea is right: a byte-level wire spec frames the query. MySQL packets, for example, start with a 3-byte length and a 1-byte sequence id. The specific byte layout in the example is illustrative, and the name 'dialect' is wrong (see L-0290).
precise_version: A database wire protocol defines byte-level message framing (e.g. MySQL packets carry a length header and sequence id, then a command byte and the SQL text). This is the wire protocol, not the SQL dialect.

note: Course/admin reference.
Correct: each protocol defines its own framing and message format.
Correct: Redis clients use RESP (RESP2/RESP3) over TCP, default port 6379.
Course/admin reference.
Personal experience claim.

Mixes two different things. A single WebSocket is one long-lived TCP connection, and an LB pins it to one backend for its whole life (AWS ALB: it 'becomes a persistent WebSocket connection between the client and the target through the load balancer'). No stickiness setting is needed for that. Sticky sessions (cookie/IP affinity) are needed when a logical session spans several HTTP requests, e.g. Socket.IO's HTTP long-polling handshake, or when you want a reconnect to land on the same node. The LB also has to support the HTTP Upgrade: nginx requires forwarding Upgrade/Connection headers explicitly.
precise_version: Behind a load balancer, each WebSocket connection is automatically pinned to one backend for its lifetime, and the LB just needs to support the HTTP Upgrade. Sticky sessions are only needed when a session spans multiple connections or requests (e.g. Socket.IO's long-polling fallback) or when reconnects must reach the same server.

note: Correct: if the LB (or LB node) fails, every connection through it drops and clients must reconnect.
Correct. Clients should reconnect with exponential backoff plus jitter to avoid a synchronized storm. Socket.IO's client does exponential backoff by default.

Reconnect storms are a well-known way to overload or cascade failure in connection-heavy systems. Each reconnect costs a TCP + TLS handshake (TLS is CPU-heavy), authentication, and often a resubscription or state resync, all landing at once on the remaining servers. These are exactly the 'retries make overload worse' dynamics AWS describes. The fix is exponential backoff with jitter, plus connection-rate limits.
precise_version: Mass reconnects after a server crash can overload the surviving servers (TLS handshakes, auth, resubscription all at once). Clients should reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter, and servers should rate-limit new connections.

note: Correct: both hold the TCP connection (long polling only until the response). The SSE connection stays open until closed.

Incomplete. The server can also end the stream deliberately. More importantly, if the connection drops for any reason the browser's EventSource reconnects automatically (after the 'retry' delay) unless the client calls close() or the server answers HTTP 204. So 'server goes down' usually leads to a reconnect, not a permanent close.
precise_version: An SSE stream ends when the client calls close(), when the server ends it, or on network or server failure. After non-deliberate drops the browser automatically reconnects and sends Last-Event-ID; a server can stop reconnection by responding 204 No Content.

note: Personal practice; not judged.

Opinion. Engineering caveat: the connection itself may be 'functional anyway', but reconnection behaviour (Last-Event-ID resume, retry timing, proxy idle timeouts and buffering) is where SSE features usually fail in production and is worth an integration test.
Correct: the EventSource API offers no way to send on the stream, even though TCP is full-duplex. Clients send data via separate HTTP requests.

Correct for L7 load balancers and proxies, which terminate the client connection and keep a separate one to the target (AWS ALB: 'one connection with the client and one connection with a target'). Some L4 balancers forward packets without terminating TCP. Then the client's TCP session effectively ends at the backend.

For pure byte relaying the choice is indeed secondary. But L4 vs L7 matters in practice for long-lived connections: idle timeouts (AWS ALB default 60 s, NLB TCP default 350 s; nginx 60 s proxy_read_timeout), TLS termination, and whether the proxy understands the HTTP Upgrade (L7) or just passes bytes (L4). Teams usually send pings or heartbeats to survive those timeouts.
Correct: L7 balancers can route on HTTP host, path and headers.
Correct and common pattern: outbound-only connections (reverse tunnel/agent) when inbound is blocked.
Opinion. Counterpoint: SSE is in heavy production use today, e.g. LLM APIs stream responses as SSE.
